newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says flu activity rising rapidly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says flu activity rising rapidly.

text.p: Influenza activity has increased rapidly in the past few weeks, dominated by a dangerous strain that hits the elderly the hardest, federal health officials said on Thursday.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said there was widespread flu activity in three states -- Colorado, Connecticut and Pennsylvania -- and regional activity in 14 others.
"We've seen a steady increase in influenza activity for about the last three weeks and we're now having outbreaks in several parts of the country," the CDC's Nancy Arden said.

The agency said 99 percent of virus specimens analyzed in the laboratory this fall have been type A(H3N2), the virus that has the most severe overall impact. Type A(H3N2) has caused about 400,000 deaths since emerging in the late 1960s. More than 90 percent of those deaths occurred among the elderly.
"We have had more than the usual number of reports of influenza type A in nursing homes," Arden said.

Regional flu outbreaks were occurring in Alaska, Arizona, Indiana, Kansas, Maryland, Montana, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Washington, during the week ending December 7. Another 25 states were reporting sporadic flu activity, the CDC said.
Two weeks earlier, only seven states were reporting regional flu activity.

Family physicians who monitor influenza as part of a "sentinel" system said 5 percent of their patient visits were due to influenza-like illnesses. In New England, the figure was 15 percent, the CDC said.

The CDC said elderly people should obtain this year's flu vaccine, which offers protection against the type A(H3N2) virus. It also said nursing homes should be ready to offer antiviral drugs such as amantadine and rimantadine which interfere with the replication of type A viruses. The drugs can reduce the severity and duration of flu illness if taken during the first two days of illness.
The CDC and the Food and Drug Administration this week recommended that people who received a flu vaccine from 11 lots of a Fluogen vaccine that were recalled in November should be reimmunized.

The vaccine was recalled because of the decreased potency in one viral strain. The agencies said only 5 percent to 7 percent of all people who received the 1996-1997 flu vaccine received doses from the recalled lots.
The Health Care Financing Administration said it would pay for Medicare beneficiaries to be reimmunized if their doctors recommended a second flu shot.
